statement: Of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less.
heath_proof: For let A have to C a greater ratio than B has to C; I say that A is greater than B. For, if not, A is either equal to B or less. Now A is not equal to B; for in that case each of the magnitudes A, B would have had the same ratio to C; [V. 7] but they have not; therefore A is not equal to B. Nor again is A less than B; for in that case A would have had to C a less ratio than B has to C; [V. 8] but it has not; therefore A is not less than B.  But it was proved not to be equal either; therefore A is greater than B.  Again, let C have to B a greater ratio than C has to A; I say that B is less than A. For, if not, it is either equal or greater. Now B is not equal to A; for in that case C would have had the same ratio to each of the magnitudes A, B; [V. 7] but it has not; therefore A is not equal to B.  Nor again is B greater than A; for in that case C would have had to B a less ratio than it has to A; [V. 8] but it has not; therefore B is not greater than A.  But it was proved that it is not equal either; therefore B is less than A.

5.10
**Statement:** Of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less.

Let A and B be two magnitudes each having a ratio to the same magnitude C.

**Part I.** Let A have to C a greater ratio than B has to C. I say that A is greater than B.

**Step 1.** Since A has to C a greater ratio than B has to C, by D5.7 there exist equimultiples mA, mB of A and B, and a multiple nC of C, such that mA exceeds nC while mB does not exceed nC.

**Step 2.** A is not equal to B. For suppose A = B. Then by 5.7 (equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio), A has to C the same ratio as B has to C. But then, by D5.5, since mA and mB are equimultiples of A and B and nC is a multiple of C, from mA > nC it would follow that mB > nC. This contradicts Step 1, in which mB does not exceed nC. Hence A is not equal to B.

**Step 3.** A is not less than B. For suppose A < B. Then by 5.8 (of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has), B has to C a greater ratio than A has to C. But by hypothesis A has to C a greater ratio than B has to C; and by D5.7 the ratio A:C is then the greater of the two ratios A:C and B:C, so it cannot at the same time be the less of them. Hence A is not less than B.

**Step 4.** Since A is neither equal to B nor less than B, A is greater than B. This proves the first part.

**Part II.** Now let C have to B a greater ratio than C has to A. I say that B is less than A.

**Step 5.** Since C has to B a greater ratio than C has to A, by D5.7 there exist a multiple mC of C (the same multiple taken as antecedent in both ratios) and equimultiples nB, nA of B and A, such that mC exceeds nB while mC does not exceed nA.

**Step 6.** B is not equal to A. For suppose B = A. Then by 5.7 (the same has to equal magnitudes the same ratio), C has to B the same ratio as C has to A. But then, by D5.5, since mC is a multiple of C and nB, nA are equimultiples of B and A, from mC > nB it would follow that mC > nA. This contradicts Step 5. Hence B is not equal to A.

**Step 7.** B is not greater than A. For suppose B > A. Then by 5.8 (the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater), C has to A a greater ratio than C has to B. But by hypothesis C has to B a greater ratio than C has to A; and by D5.7 the ratio C:B is then the greater of the two ratios C:B and C:A, so it cannot at the same time be the less of them. Hence B is not greater than A.

**Step 8.** Since B is neither equal to A nor greater than A, B is less than A. This proves the second part.

Therefore, of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less. Q.E.D.
